text: More than 200 years ago, slavery was allowed everywhere in the Americas.
Ships carried millions of Africans across the ocean to work on big farms called plantations.
src: In the 18th century slavery was legal throughout the Americas
European and American ships carried some 12.5 million Africans across the Atlantic / taken to the sugar plantations of Brazil and the Caribbean

text: In Britain, people who wanted to end slavery sent hundreds of petitions, letters signed by many people, to Parliament.
Olaudah Equiano wrote a book telling how he had been enslaved as a child.
src: The British campaigners chose to attack the slave trade first / hundreds of petitions to Parliament

Formerly enslaved writers made the case in their own words / Olaudah Equiano in his Interesting Narrative of 1789 / Olaudah Equiano wrote that he was born in what is now south-eastern Nigeria and enslaved as a child

text: In Saint-Domingue, enslaved people rose up, ended slavery there and made a new country, Haiti.
In Jamaica, tens of thousands followed a church leader, Samuel Sharpe, in a strike.
src: Enslaved people rise in Saint-Domingue; their revolution ends slavery there and founds Haiti in 1804
tens of thousands in western Jamaica followed the Baptist deacon Samuel Sharpe in a strike

text: In the United States, Harriet Tubman escaped from slavery.
Then she went back about thirteen times to lead about seventy people to freedom.
src: In the United States Frederick Douglass / Harriet Tubman, who escaped in 1849
went back some thirteen times to lead about seventy people to freedom

text: British navy ships hunted slave ships at sea and set many Africans free.
More than 130 years ago slavery ended everywhere in the Americas, but the freed rarely got land or equal rights.
src: was hunted at sea by the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron / freed some 150,000 Africans
By 1888 slavery was illegal everywhere in the Americas / freedom rarely brought the formerly enslaved land, compensation or equality

text: Historians such as Eric Williams have long argued about why slavery ended.
Today, days such as Juneteenth in the United States remember the end of slavery.
src: Historians have long argued about why abolition happened / the Trinidadian historian Eric Williams
The end of slavery is now widely commemorated / Juneteenth, on 19 June, recalls the announcement of freedom
